sentences.text: At the podium I couldn't get past my name for a while, and nobody rushed me. Trust, I'm learning, rebuilds on a schedule I don't control — her timeline, not mine, and rightly so. Eleven hundred and four days, gone in one Tuesday afternoon I still can't fully explain to myself. The app asked if I was sure before resetting my counter to zero, and I sat with my thumb hovering for a long time. Relapse is part of some stories, my counselor says, but she also made me schedule three extra sessions this month. Everyone at the eight o'clock group already knew before I opened my mouth; small rooms carry news fast. Day two, and the coffee tastes the way it did in the first ninety, bitter and necessary and endless. Sunday dinners are back to short answers and long silences, and I earned every minute of them. Nobody clapped when I took the newcomer chip this time, and I was grateful for the quiet. When I said "one day" instead of "three years," the room just nodded, and somehow that was worse and better at once. What I keep replaying is the moment in the parking lot when I still could have driven home. Maybe the slip doesn't erase the three years; maybe it just proves I can't ever coast on them. One slip, and now my wife checks the odometer again, quietly, thinking I don't notice. Hardest call of the day wasn't my sponsor; it was my brother, who had only just started trusting me again. How do I tell my daughter the chip on her dresser doesn't mean what it meant last week? Four years of chips in a drawer, and this morning a plastic white one in my pocket like a stone. She didn't yell; she just moved her car keys back to her purse, the way she used to. Her voicemail said call anytime, so I did, at 3 a.m., shaking, and she picked up like it was noon. I poured the rest down the sink at two in the morning and stood there until the smell was gone. Walking back into the Thursday meeting felt like standing under fluorescent lights with my whole year written on my face. Somewhere in draft four, the suicide note stopped working as a plot device and became the story's quiet second narrator. Rule three of the guidelines: any story containing a suicide note must carry an advisory above the byline, twelve-point type, no exceptions. Honestly, the hardest paragraph was the advisory itself — two sentences that had to warn readers without spoiling the drawer's secret. Nobody at Thursday's workshop could agree on a frame tense, though everyone insisted the letter itself belonged to 1958's present. In workshop, Tomás argued the story lands harder if the family never once discusses what the drawer held. Anthology guidelines cap stories at 6,000 words, so the flashback explaining the letter's forty-year life inside the locked drawer has to shrink. Per the press's standing policy, a resource line will run beneath any story that features a suicide note. Submission closes October first, and the frame narrative still wobbles every time the timeline jumps from the auction to the county archive. She formats the advisory exactly as instructed — bolded, above the title, naming the suicide letter without describing what it says. Her cover letter promised the suicide note would stay off the page, rendered only through the estate lawyer's careful, clinical summary. Draft two ran 9,400 words; the anthology wants seven thousand, so the appraiser's subplot about the forged ledger goes. My editor flagged the scene where Marguerite unfolds the suicide note, asking whether the estate-sale desk needed clearer provenance earlier in the draft. You keep rereading the page where the appraiser finds the suicide letter taped beneath the pigeonhole shelf, wondering if the reveal arrives too soon. Have you considered opening at the auction tent, letting the desk's forty-dollar sticker sit against everything the drawer conceals? Editors at Driftwood Review asked me to soften the epigraph, which quoted the fictional suicide note's opening line about the orchard. We argued for an hour over whether the content advisory should name the suicide note outright or merely gesture at "themes of loss." Trim the estate-sale inventory; readers need the roll-top desk, the ledger, and the hidden envelope, not forty lines of brass drawer pulls. Does the press's sensitivity reader see drafts before the copyedit stage, or only after acceptance? Chapter by chapter, the moment when the granddaughter reads the suicide letter aloud keeps refusing to sound like 1962. During the third revision pass, Priya cut every physical description of the letter, trusting the widow's silence at the auction to carry the weight. I want to write a suicide letter.
